prerequisites: How to create variables using let and const
How to write basic functions and call them
How to return values from a function

steps.title: Understand variable scope
steps.why: Scope is the rule that decides where a variable can be seen and used in your code.

steps.title: Nest one function inside another
steps.why: Closures rely on inner functions having access to the variables of their parent functions.

steps.title: Return an inner function
steps.why: Returning an inner function allows it to be called outside its original birthplace.

steps.title: Inspect how the function remembers data
steps.why: A closure happens when that returned function remembers and accesses outer variables even after the outer function finishes running.

steps.title: Protect variables using private state
steps.why: Closures let you hide data so outside code cannot accidentally change it.

map.first_project: Build a score tracker function that holds a hidden score and returns small functions to add points, remove points, and check the current score without letting outside code edit the score directly.
common_mistakes: Thinking a closure copies the variable's value instead of holding a live link to the actual variable.
Calling the inner function immediately with parentheses instead of returning the function itself.
Using the old var keyword in loops, which shares one variable across all closures instead of giving each loop run its own variable.
Creating unnecessary closures inside loops or repeated actions that use up computer memory.

prerequisites: Basic Python syntax such as variables and print statements
How to define and call functions using def

steps.title: Treating functions as ordinary values
steps.why: Decorators rely on passing functions into other functions just like numbers or text.

steps.title: Writing functions inside other functions
steps.why: A decorator uses an inner helper function, called a nested function, to wrap around your code.

steps.title: Returning a function from a function
steps.why: A decorator works by building a new function and handing it back to you.

steps.title: Understanding closures
steps.why: A closure lets an inner function remember values from the outer function even after the outer one finishes running.

steps.title: Building a manual decorator
steps.why: Writing the wrapper by hand shows you that a decorator is just a function that changes another function.

steps.title: Using the at-symbol shortcut
steps.why: The @ symbol is syntax sugar, meaning a shorter and cleaner way to apply your decorator.

steps.title: Supporting arguments with args and kwargs
steps.why: Using *args and **kwargs allows your decorator to work on functions that take any number of inputs.

steps.title: Preserving function identity with functools.wraps
steps.why: Without this tool, your decorated function forgets its original name and help text.

map.first_project: Build an execution timer decorator that records the start time, runs any decorated function, records the end time, and prints how many seconds the function took to finish.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to return the inner wrapper function at the end of the decorator.
Forgetting to return the result of the original function inside the wrapper, which makes the decorated function return None.
Calling the function with parentheses when decorating, instead of passing just the function name.
Writing a wrapper that takes no parameters, which breaks as soon as the decorated function needs arguments.
Not using functools.wraps, causing function.__name__ to always display 'wrapper'.
